etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bitte, bite, from Old English bita (“bit; fragment; morsel”) and bite (“a bite; cut”), from Proto-Germanic *bitô and *bitiz; both from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”). More at bite.

definitions.definition: A piece of metal placed in a horse's mouth and connected to the reins to direct the animal.
A rotary cutting tool fitted to a drill, used to bore holes.
(dated, British) A coin of a specified value.

(historical, US and Canada) A unit of currency worth one eighth of a dollar, originally of a Spanish dollar but later also US or Canadian; also, a coin with this value, in particular the silver Spanish real.

quote.citation: 1966 March, Thomas Pynchon, The Crying of Lot 49, New York, N.Y.: Bantam Books, published November 1976, →ISBN, page 16:
quote.text: He left after shaking her down for four bits for carrying the bags.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, US and Canada) A coin of a value similar but not equal to this, in particular the ‘short bit’, i.e. the ten-cent piece or dime.

quote.citation: 1941, Emily Carr, chapter 10, in Klee Wyck‎[3]:
quote.text: The smallest coin we had in Canada in early days was a dime, worth ten cents. The Indians called this coin “a Bit”. Our next coin, double in buying power and in size, was a twenty-five cent piece and this the Indians called “Two Bits”.

definitions.definition: (historical) A unit of currency and coin of the British West Indies worth six black dogs, originally equal to one-eighth of a Spanish dollar but later increasingly debased to one tenth, one eleventh, one twelfth, etc.

quote.citation: 1789, Olaudah Equiano, chapter 6, in The Interesting Narrative, volume I:
quote.text: I trusted to the Lord to be with me; and at one of our trips to St. Eustatia, a Dutch island, I bought a glass tumbler with my half bit, and when I came to Montserrat I sold it for a bit, or sixpence.

definitions.definition: (historical) A unit of currency of the Dutch West Indies in the early 20th century, worth one fifth of a cent.
Applied to a various small units of currency and coins.
A small amount of something.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, “The Beanspiller”, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC, page 186:
quote.text: ‘No,’ said Luke, grinning at her. ‘You're not dull enough! […] What about the kid's clothes? I don't suppose they were anything to write home about, but didn't you keep anything? A bootee or a bit of embroidery or anything at all?’

definitions.definition: (informal) Specifically, a small amount of time.
(informal) A small fraction above a whole number.
(in the plural, informal, sports) Fractions of a second.
A portion of something.

quote.citation: 2013 July-August, Catherine Clabby, “Focus on Everything”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: Not long ago, it was difficult to produce photographs of tiny creatures with every part in focus. […] A photo processing technique called focus stacking has changed that. Developed as a tool to electronically combine the sharpest bits of multiple digital images, focus stacking is a boon to biologists seeking full focus on a micron scale.

definitions.definition: Somewhat; something, but not very great; also used like jot and whit to express the smallest degree. See also a bit.

quote.text: My young companion was a bit of a poet.

definitions.definition: (slang) A prison sentence, especially a short one.

quote.citation: 1904, The Anamosa prison press, volume 7, Iowa. Colony of Detention at Anamosa:
quote.text: Had it not been for the influence of Mrs. Booth and Hope Hall I should still be grafting or doing a bit in some stir

quote.citation: 1916, Thomas Mott Osborne. Warden, Sing Sing Prison, N. Y., “Prison Reform”, in The Journal of sociologic medicine, volume 17, page 407:
quote.text: Before doing that I am going to tell you what was the result of my own incarceration, because I presume it may not be a secret to you, that I have done a "bit" myself, not the "bit" which the prosecuting attorney was so anxious to have me do.

Chino didn't make me think of Dachau or that notorious joint in Angola, Louisiana, where a brother who had done a bit there told me how they used to cut the grass on the front lawn with their fingernails.
Not counting the days—that's okay for a county-time slap, but it'll make you crazy if you've got years to go on a felony bit.

definitions.definition: An excerpt of material making up part of a show, comedy routine, etc.
(slang) A gag or put-on; a humorous conceit, especially when insistently presented as true.

quote.citation: 2024 March 1, F1NN5TER, 3:36 from the start, in Coming Out‎[4], archived from the original on 14 May 2024:
quote.text: Also, I'm bi.  I like dudes!  ...That's weird to say.  Everything I say feels like a bit now, god dammit.

definitions.definition: Short for bit part.
The part of a key which enters the lock and acts upon the bolt and tumblers.[1]
The cutting iron of a plane.[2]
The bevelled front edge of an axehead along which the cutting edge runs.
(BDSM) A gag of a style similar to a bridle.
(MLE) A gun.

quote.citation: 2013 December 23, Stephen Reynolds, 46:53 from the start, in Stephen Reynolds, director, Vendetta (film), spoken by Jimmy Vickers (Danny Dyer):
quote.text: Jimmy: I need to get my hands on some bits. If you’re still in the business.Ronnie (played by Nick Nevern): Oi!Trojan (played by Jean-Paul Van Cauwelaert): Ronnie. […] Trojan: Now that is a SIG Sauer P226.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To put a bridle upon; to put the bit in the mouth of (a horse).
simple past of bite
(informal in US, archaic in UK) past participle of bite, bitten
(chiefly in combination) Having been bitten.

quote.citation: 1984 July, Field & Stream, volume 89, number 3, page 24:
quote.text: Fortunately, someone who gets skeeter-bit this much may develop an immunity to the skeeter's saliva

quote.citation: 1992, Robert Lewis Taylor, The Travels of Jaimie McPheeters‎[5]:
quote.text: Only the year before, the conjure man had brought in the Jackson County madstone, from way over in Illinois, for a white peddler that had been dog-bit, and the man went ahead and died just the same
He will not — he'll tell you not to be loco, climbing up trees late at night when you'll get bug-bit to death plus you can't see anything

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Coined by John Tukey in 1946 as an abbreviation of binary digit, probably influenced by connotations of “small portion”. First used in print 1948 by Claude Shannon. Compare byte and nybble, with similar food associations.

definitions.definition: (mathematics, computing) A binary digit, generally represented as a 1 or 0.
(computing) The smallest unit of storage in a digital computer, consisting of a binary digit.
(information theory, cryptography) Any datum that may take on one of exactly two values.
(information theory) A unit of measure for information entropy.

quote.citation: 2011 May 17, Lisa Grossman, “Entropy Is Universal Rule of Language”, in Wired Science‎[7], retrieved 2012-09-26:
quote.text: The researchers found that the original texts spanned a variety of entropy values in different languages, reflecting differences in grammar and structure.But strangely, the difference in entropy between the original, ordered text and the randomly scrambled text was constant across languages. This difference is a way to measure the amount of information encoded in word order, Montemurro says. The amount of information lost when they scrambled the text was about 3.5 bits per word.

definitions.definition: A microbitcoin, or a millionth of a bitcoin (0.000001 BTC).
